newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Treasurer asks SEC probe of bond deals.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Treasurer asks SEC probe of bond deals.

text.p: California state Treasurer Matt Fong has called on the Securities and Exchange Commission and the state attorney general to investigate several municipal securities transactions in the state.
Fong called for the investigations in letters to SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt and Attorney General Dan Lungren.
The letters were released Thursday at a meeting of the California Debt Advisory Commission.
"I am writing to request your investigation of certain recent municipal securities transactions in California that threaten the integrity of the municipal market," Fong said in his letter to Levitt.

Fong referred to a series of transactions conducted under the state's Marks-Roos Local Bond Pooling Act, which authorises the formation of joint powers agencies to finance capital projects of local government agencies.
Fong's office said it included nine deals underwritten by Pacific Genesis Group Inc.
An official with the firm in San Francisco declined to comment, saying he had yet to see Fong's letters.
In these transactions, the joint powers agencies were formed by local governments in return for a cash payment from the bond proceeds.

The bond proceeds were represented as being used to pay for public capital improvements in other areas of the state but in fact were first used to retire loans against the developer's private property, Fong said.
Indian tribes were represented to be the "local agencies" on whose behalf the bonds were issued, Fong said.
He said these offerings violated the "letter and spirit" of state law.
"In my view, these practices violate state laws, raise federal securities law concerns, and harm the interests of the issuer community in general," Fong said in the letter.
Fong said these bond sales appear to have been conducted in violation of state laws for essentially private purposes.

"If federal and state securities laws are not enforced against those persons responsible for these transactions, others may be encouraged to undertake even more creative, risky, and illegal transactions in the future," Fong said in his letter to the SEC.
Fong sent similar letters to Lungren, as well as officials with the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board, an industry regulatory panel in Washington, and the California State Bar Association.
